title: Spell Formula 1: Defining a function
lessonSummary: Great! You wrote your first spell formula and cast it several times.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: One formula is defined once and called twice.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def greet_hero():
    print("Welcome, brave hero!")
    print("Your adventure begins now!")

greet_hero()
greet_hero()

tasks.instruction: Define a function cast_spell() that prints exactly Fireball! and call it three times.
Define a function heal() that prints exactly You are healed! Call it once, then print exactly Done! (outside the function).

title: Spell Formula 1: One parameter
lessonSummary: Nice! Your spell formula can now work with different ingredients.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The same formula greets two different heroes.
Write a function cast_spell(spell) that prints You cast: <spell>! Call it with "Fireball" and then with "Lightning".

validation.expected:
You cast: Fireball!
You cast: Lightning!

tasks.instruction: Write a function show_level(level) that prints Level: <level> Call it with the numbers 5 and 12 (without quotes).

title: Spell Formula 1: Several parameters
lessonSummary: Great! Your formulas now take several ingredients in the right order.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: Three arguments fill three parameters – in the right order.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def create_character(name, class_name, level):
    print(f"Name: {name}")
    print(f"Class: {class_name}")
    print(f"Level: {level}")

create_character("Aria", "Mage", 5)

tasks.instruction: Write a function strike(weapon, damage) that prints You hit with <weapon> for <damage> damage! Call it with ("Sword", 12) and then with ("Axe", 20).

validation.expected:
You hit with Sword for 12 damage!
You hit with Axe for 20 damage!

tasks.instruction: The function trade_goods(given, received) is already finished. Call it so that it prints exactly You trade 2 herbs for 1 potion Watch the order of the arguments!

title: Spell Formula 2: Returning values with return
lessonSummary: Magical! Your formulas now deliver results you can keep calculating with.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The result is stored and used right away.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_damage(base, multiplier):
    return base * multiplier

damage = calculate_damage(10, 2)
print(f"Hit: {damage} damage")
print(f"Critical: {calculate_damage(20, 5)} damage")

tasks.instruction: Write a function double(number) that returns number * 2 with return. Then print exactly Double: 42 by using double(21).
Write a function calculate_mana(level, base_mana) that returns level * base_mana. Store calculate_mana(4, 10) in the variable mana and print exactly Mana: 40

title: Spell Formula 2: return or print?
lessonSummary: Well spotted! You now know when a formula prints and when it returns.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: A function without return gives back None.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def show_inventory():
    print("Sword, Shield, Healing Potion")

result = show_inventory()
print(f"Return value: {result}")

tasks.instruction: The function calculate_loot calculates the loot but does not return it – that is why it prints Loot: None. Add return so that exactly Loot: 42 is printed.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_loot(gold, silver):
    total = gold + silver

loot = calculate_loot(30, 12)
print(f"Loot: {loot}")

tasks.instruction: Write a function total_cost(price, amount) that returns price * amount. Use it: total = total_cost(15, 4), gold = 100 - total. Print exactly Gold left: 40

title: Spell Formula 2: Decisions and loops in functions
lessonSummary: Masterful! Your formulas can now decide and repeat.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The function returns a different text depending on the level.
Write a function is_strong(damage) that returns True if damage is at least 50, otherwise False. Print is_strong(80) and then is_strong(20) with print.
Write a function sum_to(n) that adds all numbers from 1 to n with a for loop and returns the sum. Print exactly Sum: 55 by using sum_to(10).

title: Spell Formula 3: Docstrings and good names
lessonSummary: Excellent! Your formulas now have descriptions and good names.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The docstring is shown with __doc__.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_healing(base, multiplier):
    """Calculates the amount of healing."""
    return base * multiplier

print(calculate_healing.__doc__)
print(calculate_healing(10, 2))

tasks.instruction: Write a function show_title() with the docstring "Shows the hero's title." (in triple quotes) that prints Master of Spell Formulas First print show_title.__doc__, then call the function.

validation.expected:
Shows the hero's title.
Master of Spell Formulas

tasks.instruction: The function is called cd(b, m) – a bad name. Rename it to calculate_damage(base, multiplier) (also the parameters in the body) so the call below works and prints exactly Damage: 21

title: Debug Quest
lessonSummary: All bugs found! With functions, indentation, the parentheses on the call and return matter.

tasks.instruction: 🐛 Bug #1 – Goal: The program should print Welcome, hero! What is wrong?
🐛 Bug #2 – Goal: The program should print Damage: 10 (for strength 5). What is wrong?
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_damage(strength):
    return strength * 2

result = calculate_damage
print(f"Damage: {result}")

tasks.instruction: 🐛 Bug #3 – Goal: The program should print Sum: 8. What is wrong?
tasks.codeTemplate:
def add(a, b):
    result = a + b

total = add(5, 3)
print(f"Sum: {total}")

title: Mission 1: The Spell Apprentice
lessonSummary: The Spell Apprentice is trained: You wrote formulas, called them and delivered results!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Greeting spell: Write a function greet_mage() that prints exactly Welcome, mage! Call it twice.
Step 2 – Mana calculation: Write a function calculate_mana(level, base_mana) that returns level * base_mana. Print exactly Mana: 60 by using calculate_mana(5, 12).

Step 3 – Spell possible? Write a function is_spell_possible(mana_cost, current_mana) that returns True if current_mana is at least mana_cost, otherwise False. Print Fireball: True (cost 30, mana 50) and then Lightning: False (cost 40, mana 25).

title: Mission 2: The Character Smith
lessonSummary: The Character Smith is done: Your functions now build complete heroes!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Health: Write a function calculate_health(level, class_name) that returns level * 20 for the class "Warrior" and level * 10 for every other class. Print exactly Warrior: 60 (level 3) and Mage: 30 (level 3) with it.
Step 2 – Title: Write a function create_title(name, class_name) that returns the text <name> the <class_name>. Print exactly Aria the Mage by printing create_title("Aria", "Mage").

Step 3 – Character sheet: The functions from steps 1 and 2 are provided. Write show_character_sheet(name, class_name, level) that prints three lines: the title, Health: <health> and Level: <level>. Call it with ("Thorin", "Warrior", 4).

title: Mission 3: The Quest Machine
lessonSummary: The Quest Machine is running: Reward, requirement and display work hand in hand!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Reward: Write a function calculate_reward(difficulty) that returns difficulty * 50. Print exactly Reward: 150 by using calculate_reward(3).

Step 2 – Requirement: Write a function can_do_quest(level, difficulty) that returns True if level is at least difficulty * 2, otherwise False. Print Quest 3: True (level 8) and then Quest 5: False (level 8).

Step 3 – Quest display: The two functions are provided. Write show_quest(name, difficulty, level): It prints <name>: reward <reward> if the hero may do the quest, otherwise <name>: too hard. Call it with ("Dragon Hunt", 4, 9) and ("Treasure Hunt", 2, 3).

validation.expected:
Dragon Hunt: reward 200
Treasure Hunt: too hard

title: Extra Challenge 1: The Spell Generator
lessonSummary: The Spell Generator runs: Names, power and display fit together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Spell name: Write a function spell_name(element, level) that returns the text <element>-L<level>. Print exactly Spell: FIRE-L3 by using spell_name("FIRE", 3).

Step 2 – Power: Write a function calculate_power(element, level): For "FIRE" the power is level * 30, for "WATER" level * 20, for everything else level * 15. At level 3 print FIRE: 90, WATER: 60 and EARTH: 45 (each calculated, in this order).
Step 3 – Generator: Both functions are provided. Write show_spell(element, level) that prints <name> has power <power>, and call it in a for loop for FIRE with the levels 1 to 3.

validation.expected:
FIRE-L1 has power 30
FIRE-L2 has power 60
FIRE-L3 has power 90

title: Extra Challenge 2: The Guild Manager
lessonSummary: The Guild Manager stands: Costs, budget and report work together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Costs: Write a function calculate_costs(mages, days) that returns mages * days * 5. Print exactly Costs: 150 by using calculate_costs(6, 5).

Step 2 – Affordable? Write a function is_affordable(costs, gold) that returns True if gold is at least costs, otherwise False. Print Affordable: True (costs 150, gold 200) and then Affordable: False (costs 150, gold 100).

Step 3 – Report: Both functions are provided. Write guild_report(department, mages, days, gold) that prints three lines: Department <department>, Costs: <costs> and Affordable: <True/False>. Call it with ("Fire", 6, 5, 200).

title: Extra Challenge 3: The Battle Simulation
lessonSummary: The Battle Simulation runs: Damage, rounds and result fit together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Damage: Write a function calculate_damage(base, armor) that returns base - armor, but never less than 0. Print Damage: 25 (base 40, armor 15) and then Damage: 0 (base 10, armor 30).

Step 2 – Battle round: Write a function battle_round(health, damage) that returns the new health (health - damage, but never below 0). Start with health = 100, call battle_round(health, 25) twice (store the result in health again) and print Health: <health> after each call.

Step 3 – Battle: battle_round is provided. Write simulate_battle(health, damage, rounds): A for loop (round 1 to rounds) calls battle_round each time and prints Round <number>: Health <health> At the end the function returns the health. Call it with (100, 30, 4), store the result in final and print Final: <final>

validation.expected:
Round 1: Health 70
Round 2: Health 40
Round 3: Health 10
Round 4: Health 0
Final: 0
